summary: The 13th Dalai Lama worked in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied under teachers including Agvan Dorjiev, Terton Sogyal, Pa Ri Rabsal, and Yeshe Chopel, and taught numerous students, including Chogye Trichen Rinpoche and the 9th Panchen Lama.

Working in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Tibetology, he studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche, Trijang Rinpoche, Ling Rinpoche, and others. He founded the International Network of Engaged Buddhists (1989) and the Mind and Life Institute (1990).
Active in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, he studied under Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, Kalu Rinpoche in 1973, and Khenchen Thrangu Rinpoche.
Specializing in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, he studied under Jamphel Yeshe Gyaltsen, Ngawang Lobzang Gyatso, and Khangsar Dorje Chang.

id: P:3rd Sras Rinpoche Thubten Kalsang Bstanpai Gyaltsen
summary: In Tibetology and Buddhist studies, he studied under the 96th Ganden Tripa Thubten Kunga, at Drepung Loseling Monastery (1950–1971), and at Gyume Tantric College (1971). He later held posts at Rizong, Drepung Loseling (1984), and Gyume (1995–2008).

id: P:7th Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche Karma Sungrab Ngedön Tenpe Gyeltshen
summary: Active in Buddhist studies and Tibetology, he served as director at the Kamalashila Institute and founded both Nitartha International and Nalandabodhi.
He studied under Shenphen Nangwa and Thubten Chökyi Dorje.
He studied under Khenpo Ngawang Pelzang, Thubten Chökyi Dorje, and Ayu Khandro, and taught Nyoshul Khenpo Jamyang Dorje.
He studied at Pachaiyappa's College from around 1908 to 1911. He later held posts at Pachaiyappa's College (1911–1918) and served as a professor at the University of Mysore (1918–1947).
An Indologist, he served as a Senior Dakshina Fellow at Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute and as a lecturer on Sanskrit at Karnatak Arts College Dharwad.

Working in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and computational fields, he earned a PhD at Stony Brook under Sung-Bae Park. He held posts at Toyo Gakuen (1994–2008), University of Tokyo (2008–2019), and Musashino University (2019).
Active in Indology, he studied under Tirumalai Krishnamacharya from around 1971 to 1989 and founded the Krishnamacharya Yoga Mandiram in 1976.

Working in history, archaeology, and philosophy, he studied at Alexandria University, London School of Economics, and under Karl Popper. He held academic posts at the Warburg Institute (1962–1972) and Harvard University (1972–1996).

A scholar in linguistics and Indology, he studied at Mysore and completed his PhD at Indiana University. He held positions at Baroda, Deccan College, and notably the University of Chicago from 1962, becoming William E. Colvin Professor in 1983.

Specializing in Indology and Buddhist studies, he completed his doctorate at SOAS under John Brough around 1949–1954. He held posts at the University of Edinburgh (1955–1963) and the University of Toronto (1963–1990).
A scholar of linguistics and Indology, he earned his PhD at SOAS under Ralph Lilley Turner (~1930–1933). He held posts at the University of Mysore and Maharaja's College, Mysore.
An Indologist who succeeded Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar, he served as Professor of Sanskrit at Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute (attested 2026).
A scholar in Buddhist and religious studies, he earned his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1984 and later held a post at the University of Calgary (attested 1998).

Specializing in Buddhist studies and Japanology, he earned his PhD at the University of Michigan under Micah L. Auerback (~2010–2015). Around 2015, he became assistant professor of Japanese Studies at the University at Albany, SUNY.

Working in history and archaeology, he studied at Sanskrit Collegiate School, Sanskrit College and University, and Government College of Art & Craft. He held a post at the University of Calcutta from around 1921 to 1929.
